title: Lamed-Aleph Verbs
description: Learn the final-radical aleph and its quiescence.

blocks.caption: Summary
blocks.html: Lamed-Aleph verbs end in aleph. At the end of a syllable the aleph is silent, and the vowel before it is lengthened because the syllable has become effectively open. The class tends to fall together with Lamed-He verbs, and the two are frequently confused in spelling.

blocks.caption: The final aleph
blocks.html: When aleph closes a syllable it is silent after the preceding vowel, which lengthens: מָצָא (he found) from a form in which the aleph is not sounded. In the perfect of active verbs the a is kept throughout; in the perfect of stative verbs, and in the other stems, the vowel is e. All imperfects and imperatives take e before the aleph.

blocks.caption: Confusion with Lamed-He
blocks.html: This class has a strong tendency to adopt the vocalisation, and even the spelling, of Lamed-He verbs — "to heal" may be written with either final letter, and the roots "to call" and "to meet" are sometimes confused. This is a genuine feature of the class, so do not force a rigid distinction in every form.

blocks.caption: Common confusion
blocks.html: Do not read the final aleph as a consonant. It is usually silent and only lengthens the vowel before it. Because of the frequent overlap with Lamed-He, compare the two classes rather than insisting that every form be one or the other.

blocks.caption: Worked example
blocks.html: Take מָצָא ("he found"). The final aleph is silent, and the a before it lengthens because the syllable is effectively open. Read the aleph as lengthening the vowel, not as a consonant, and watch for the overlap with Lamed-He spelling.

blocks.caption: Reading practice
blocks.html: Read and parse. מָצָא הָאִישׁ — "the man found". קָרָא הָעָם — "the people called". The final aleph is silent and lengthens the vowel before it; read it as a vowel-carrier, not a consonant.
